subject: Geography
title: Mountains, Plateaus and Valleys
learningOutcomes: Identify and explain the formation of fold, block, residual and volcanic mountains.
Locate the Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindu Kush ranges and describe their importance.
Explain why earthquakes occur frequently in Pakistan and how the Himalayas keep growing.
Differentiate a plateau from a mountain and identify the Potohar and Balochistan plateaus.
Differentiate V-shaped, U-shaped and rift valleys and name the famous valleys of Pakistan.

sections.heading: What Are Mountains and How Do They Form?
sections.body: A mountain is a large landform that rises steeply above its surroundings, to a peak or ridge above 600 metres. There are four types based on how they form. Fold mountains form when two plates collide and soft sedimentary rocks bend or buckle up through folding due to compressional forces (the Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies and Urals). Block mountains form by faulting, when the side blocks are pushed down and the central block is pushed up; a block mountain with a flat top is a horst. Residual mountains are the harder rocks left behind after long weathering and erosion (Girnar hills, Nilgiri hills, Sierra of Spain). Volcanic mountains form when volcanoes erupt and pile layers of magma on the surface (Mount Fuji, Vesuvius, Kilimanjaro, Pinatubo, Erebus, Rainer, Saint Helen).

sections.heading: Mountains of Pakistan
sections.body: Pakistan has beautiful mountains in the North and West. The Himalayas are like a wall separating the subcontinent from central Asia and extend nearly 320 km into Pakistan, splitting (south to north) into the Pir Panjal, Zaskar and Ladakh ranges. To the north lies the Karakoram and to its west the Hindu Kush. Melting snow feeds the rivers: the Jhelum (from Pir Panjal), the Indus (from Zaskar and Ladakh) and the Shyok (from the Karakoram). The Karakoram Highway, the highest paved road, is called the eighth wonder of the world and is the only overland link between Pakistan and China. The Hindu Kush Himalaya holds the largest volume of ice and snow outside the Arctic and Antarctica and is the world's most important water tower.

sections.heading: Why Earthquakes Occur in Pakistan
sections.body: Pakistan lies at the boundary of two continental plates, the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate, which cuts through the centre of the country in a north-east to south-west direction. Because both plates have the same density, folding occurred and formed the Himalayan fold mountains. Convergent movement still continues, so the Himalayas rise about 1 cm every year and earthquakes occur frequently. One of Pakistan's deadliest earthquakes struck Azad Jammu and Kashmir in 2005, measuring 7.6 on the Richter Scale and leaving about 79,000 people dead.

sections.heading: Plateaus
sections.body: A plateau is a raised, flat-surfaced landform, also called table land or a flat-topped mountain, ranging from about 500 metres to thousands of metres in height. Rivers, water and wind can cut through a plateau and expose its rock layers, as the Colorado River did to carve the Grand Canyon Plateau in the USA. Plateaus cover 45% of the Earth's land surface; the Tibetan Plateau in Central Asia is the largest and highest, at about 4,500 metres, and is called the roof of the Earth. Pakistan has two major plateaus: the Potohar Plateau (bounded by the Jhelum on the East, the Indus on the West, the Margalla Hills on the North and the Salt Range on the South) and the Balochistan Plateau (west of the Sulaiman and Kirthar ranges).

sections.heading: Valleys
sections.body: A valley is a long depression surrounded by higher ground on the sides. V-shaped valleys are cut by rivers and streams into narrow, steep shapes (river valleys) — the Chitral Valley (1,128 m, reached through the Shandur Pass, home of the world's highest polo ground) is an example. U-shaped valleys are eroded and widened by glaciers into broad shapes (glacier valleys). A rift valley is an elongated lowland between two highlands formed by faulting, such as the East African Rift Valley system, where valleys 30 to 60 km wide and long narrow lakes show the land sinking due to tensional forces.

sections.heading: Famous Valleys, Lifestyles and the Importance of the Himalayas
sections.body: Famous valleys of Pakistan include Chitral and Kaghan (KPK), Murree (Himalaya range, about 30 km northeast of Islamabad, built during British rule), Hunza (Gilgit Baltistan, with the Ladyfinger peak), Bagrot (Karakoram range, known for fruits and vegetables) and Naran (KPK, 2500 m above sea level). People at high altitude face harsh conditions: Ahmed farms on terraces and travels by jeep or donkey; Faisal grows wheat and cotton on the Potohar Plateau (rich in limestone, rock salt and marble) and works at the Attock oil refinery; Abdullah near the Pir Panjal does trans-human farming. The Himalayas are rich in minerals and, with the Karakoram, act as a barrier for the monsoon winds, affecting Pakistan's precipitation pattern.

definitions.definition: A large landform that rises steeply above its surroundings, to a peak or ridge above 600 metres.
Mountains formed when two plates collide and soft sedimentary rocks bend or buckle up (e.g. the Himalayas).
Mountains formed by faulting when the side blocks are pushed down and the central block is pushed up.
A block mountain with a flat top.
The harder rocks left behind after long weathering and erosion (e.g. Nilgiri hills).
Mountains formed when volcanoes erupt and pile layers of magma on the surface.
A raised, flat-surfaced landform, also called table land or a flat-topped mountain.
A long depression surrounded by higher ground on the sides.
A narrow, steep valley cut by rivers and streams, also called a river valley.
A broad valley eroded and widened by glaciers, also called a glacier valley.
An elongated lowland between two highlands formed by faulting.
The highest paved road, called the eighth wonder of the world and the only overland link between Pakistan and China.

examTips: Learn the four mountain types by their process: folding = fold mountains, faulting = block mountains, weathering & erosion = residual mountains, volcanic eruption = volcanic mountains.
Remember Pakistan's faults by region: Chaman (west), Pab (south), Main Mantle Thrust (north).
V-shaped valleys are cut by rivers (river valleys); U-shaped valleys are widened by glaciers (glacier valleys); rift valleys form by faulting.
Key numbers: mountain above 600 m, Himalayas 40–50 million years old rising 1 cm/year, 2005 quake 7.6 (~79,000 dead), plateaus 45% of land, Tibetan Plateau ~4,500 m.
